newsitem.title: UK: Charity says UK welfare-to-work needs guarantees.
newsitem.headline: Charity says UK welfare-to-work needs guarantees.

text.p: A leading British charity said on Tuesday that for Labour's "welfare to work" scheme to succeed, adequate childcare for lone parents, training schemes and adequate jobs must be provided.
But it broadly welcomed the attempt to get 250,000 young jobless into employment.

"In order for it to work other things need to be in place, such as training schemes, such as childcare, such as jobs," Child Poverty Action Group (CPAG) director Sally Witcher said. "But in general the welfare to work scheme is a good objective to have."

Britain's Labour government has pledged to tackle youth unemployment through a three billion pound "welfare to work" programme that will form the centrepiece of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's budget on Wednesday.

Under the plan, which aims to put 250,000 18-24 year-olds into full-time employment, employers will be paid 60 pounds a week for taking on a person in that age group who has been out of work for more than six months.

The subsidy is 75 pounds for employing someone who has not been in gainful employment for more than two years. It will be funded by a windfall tax on what the government calls the excess profits of Britain's privatised utilities.
Witcher said CPAG was worried there might not be any jobs available, that it may not be feasible for single-parents to work, or simply that work does not necessarily mean an escape from poverty.

The plan would offer young people four options -- a job, a training place, work on an environmental taskforce or a placement with a voluntary organisation. But those who refuse to take any of the options would be penalised.

"If there are quality options there then it is quite reasonable to argue that they have to do things in return for the benefit," Witcher said. "We would need to be convinced that the options really were there."

There is a possibility that the scheme will penalise those who are eligible and qualified for a job but do not fit into the government's target group, or subsidise employment of people who would have got the job anyway, Witcher said.
"You would need to watch very carefully not only the effects on (benefit) claimants but also on the labour market," she said.

The programme would also rest on the government's ability to provide adequate childcare for single parents for whom a job is not feasible unless provision can be provided. "Childcare is a major barrier for lone parents getting into work," Witcher said.

She added that it was fundamental that Labour honoured its pledge to introduce a national healthcare strategy to allow families to balance their working and home responsibilities for the scheme to work.
"If the national healthcare strategy comes to pass then that will make a very big difference," she said.
